title: Efficient DCQO Algorithm within the Impulse Regime for Portfolio Optimization
abstract_summary: The authors propose a faster digitized-counterdiabatic quantum optimization (DCQO) algorithm operating in the impulse regime—where counterdiabatic terms dominate—to reduce circuit depth and improve solution accuracy for portfolio optimization. They demonstrate both purely quantum and hybrid (h-DCQO) versions on a 20-asset real dataset, benchmark against QAOA and digitized-adiabatic methods, and experimentally validate advantages on IonQ hardware, reporting circuit-depth reductions of 2.5–40× and reduced reliance on classical optimization.
methodology_description: The authors develop and evaluate a digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization (DCQO) protocol operating in the impulse (fast non-adiabatic) regime for combinatorial portfolio optimization. They map a single-period Markowitz portfolio optimization problem with a budget constraint into an Ising problem Hamiltonian Hf (coefficients hi, Jij computed from historical returns and covariances and Lagrange multipliers). They derive a first-order analytic approximation of the adiabatic gauge potential A_lambda using a single nested commutator and obtain an analytic expression for the CD coefficient alpha1. The continuous-time CD-assisted Hamiltonian H(t) = (1-lambda)Hi + lambda Hf + dot(lambda) A_lambda is digitized via first-order Trotterization with step size dt and N steps. In the impulse regime (|dot(lambda)| >> |lambda|) they keep only the Trotter steps where the CD term is dominant, apply a gate-angle cutoff (threshold 0.1) to remove small-angle rotations, and transpile logical gates to IonQ native gates (GPi, GPi2, MS). They evaluate both a purely quantum DCQO (CD term only) and a hybrid variational h-DCQO (ansatz composed solely of CD layers parameterized by single- and two-body CD coefficients), comparing to QAOA and digitized-adiabatic evolution baselines. Hybrid variational training used COBYLA (up to 200 iterations) via the Tequila framework. Experiments include simulations (Amazon Braket SDK) and runs on IonQ Aria (25-qubit trapped-ion QPU via AWS Braket) with debias error mitigation and 5000 shots. Performance is reported using a mean-based approximation ratio r(avg) = (Eavg - E)/(Eavg - Emin) and via energy distributions.
experimental_setup: Simulations implemented with Amazon Braket SDK. Hardware experiments executed on IonQ Aria (25-qubit fully connected trapped-ion QPU) accessed via AWS Braket. Hybrid variational training performed locally using Tequila with COBYLA optimizer (max 200 iterations). Error mitigation: debias. Shots per circuit: 5000. Gate-angle cutoff threshold: 0.1. Trotter step size dt = 0.1 (examples).
dataset_used: Historical stock prices for 20 assets (AAPL, JPM, JNJ, AMZN, PG, XOM, BA, DD, T, NEE, AMT, UPS, HD, PFE, NVDA, MSFT, GILD, GM, BRK-B, LMT) covering the period 06.06.2022 to 01.01.2023. Markowitz single-period model with budget B = n/2 and Lagrange multipliers theta1=1, theta2=0.5, theta3=2 to compute Ising coefficients.

experiment_input.problem_encoding: Markowitz single-period objective converted to Ising form (hi, Jij) using Eq. (2) with Lagrange multipliers theta1=1, theta2=0.5, theta3=2; budget B = n/2
experiment_input.preprocessing: Compute expected returns and covariance from historical prices, assemble quadratic binary cost, map to Ising Hamiltonian coefficients (hi, Jij).

pipeline_steps: Assemble problem Hamiltonian Hf from Markowitz model and historical data (compute hi and Jij).
Choose initial Hamiltonian Hi = -sum Xi and scheduling lambda(t) with lambda(0)=0, lambda(T)=1 (given smooth schedule).
Compute first-order approximation of adiabatic gauge potential A_lambda via a single nested commutator and derive analytic alpha1 (Appendix A).

Digitize the CD-assisted dynamics via first-order Trotterization with step size dt and N steps; identify impulse-regime steps where CD term dominates (|dot(lambda)| large) and keep p dominant steps (drop q steps with negligible CD contribution).
Apply gate-angle cutoff (threshold 0.1) to remove rotations with small angles; transpile logical gates to IonQ native gate set (GPi, GPi2, MS) using specified decompositions.
For purely quantum DCQO: run CD-only Trotterized circuit (examples: 7 Trotter steps which after cutoff reduce to 1 effective step) in simulation and on IonQ device.

For hybrid h-DCQO: build a variational ansatz composed solely of CD layers, parameterized by single- and two-qubit CD parameters (alpha, beta); perform classical optimization of expectation value <Hf> using Tequila + COBYLA (≤200 iterations) locally to find optimal parameters; run optimized circuit on IonQ device.
Compare baselines: QAOA (p=1 and p=5), digitized-adiabatic evolution (example 80 steps), and non-adiabatic without CD.
Collect measurement outcomes (5000 shots), compute energy distributions and mean-based approximation ratio r(avg), and apply debias error mitigation to hardware results.

reproducibility_notes: The paper specifies frameworks and device configurations (AWS Braket, IonQ Aria, Tequila, Qiskit) and gives analytic expressions and gate decomposition details, but does not provide a public code repository or data processing scripts. The financial data are public (Yahoo Finance) and the methods (parameter values, dt, gate cutoff, optimization settings) are documented, so reproduction is feasible given access to the same cloud services and hardware, but exact experiment scripts and seeds are not published in the preprint.
key_findings: [supported] The authors propose a DCQO (digitized-counterdiabatic quantum optimization) protocol operating in the impulse regime where the counterdiabatic (CD) term dominates, and demonstrate this protocol reduces required circuit depth while maintaining solution quality for portfolio optimization.

[supported] Pure DCQO (CD-only ansatz) on a 20-asset portfolio matches the performance of a finite-time digitized-adiabatic evolution: 7 DCQO steps (effectively 1 step after gate cut-off) achieved r(avg) ≈ 0.54, comparable to 80 adiabatic Trotter steps (r(avg) ≈ 0.53).

[supported] Experimental implementation on IonQ trapped-ion hardware (Aria) with up to 20 qubits: DCQO achieved r(avg) = 0.40 (unmitigated), r(avg) = 0.50 (with debias error mitigation), while simulation gives r(avg) ≈ 0.54.

[supported] Benchmarking on 1000 random Ising spin-glass instances (10–20 qubits) shows DCQO (CD-only) outperforms non-CD non-adiabatic evolution at fixed circuit depth, with roughly a 2× increase in the mean-based approximation ratio in the reported tests.

[supported] The hybrid h-DCQO (variational ansatz composed only of CD terms, one parameter per CD term) achieves competitive performance with fewer layers: one layer of h-DCQO achieved r(avg) ≈ 0.72 on the 20-asset instance, comparable to QAOA with p=5 (r(avg) ≈ 0.73), implying fewer variational layers/parameters are needed.

[supported] The authors report a compression in circuit requirements: compared to QAOA, h-DCQO required ~5× fewer layers (leading to ~2.5× reduction in circuit depth accounting for per-layer depth differences) to reach similar approximation ratios in their experiments.

[supported] A practical gate-reduction strategy (thresholding small rotation angles, e.g., cutoff 0.1) is effective in the impulse regime to prune negligible gates and reduce depth; this was used in their DCQO hardware runs.

[supported] Applying simple error mitigation (debias) improved hardware results noticeably for DCQO and h-DCQO, bringing mitigated hardware outputs closer to noiseless simulation for low-depth circuits.

[speculative] The authors claim the method is applicable to a large class of combinatorial optimization problems beyond portfolio optimization; this is asserted based on the Ising formulation but not exhaustively demonstrated.

[speculative] The paper suggests that operating in the impulse regime and using CD-only ansatzes can generally minimize dependence on classical optimization subroutines and reduce variational parameter counts; while supported for their instances (reduced parameter count), the generality of this claim across problems/hardware is not proven here.

[speculative] The authors propose that a digital-analog approach may further enhance practical utility in the NISQ era; this is suggested as future direction rather than empirically established in the work.
results_summary: The paper introduces DCQO and a hybrid variant h-DCQO that leverage first-order counterdiabatic terms in the impulse (fast-evolution) regime to compress quantum circuits for portfolio optimization. In simulation and on IonQ trapped-ion hardware (up to 20 qubits), the authors show that a CD-only ansatz can match the performance of much deeper digitized-adiabatic evolutions and outperform non-CD approaches at fixed depth. For a 20-asset instance, 7 DCQO steps (reducible to 1 via gate cut-off) reached r(avg) ≈ 0.54, similar to 80-step adiabatic evolution. The hybrid h-DCQO achieved r(avg) ≈ 0.72 with one variational layer, comparable to QAOA with five layers, indicating significant layer/parameter compression. Error mitigation improved hardware fidelity but deeper h-DCQO circuits still showed gaps to simulation, motivating further noise-suppression work. The authors claim applicability to broader combinatorial problems, though that remains to be validated more widely.
performance_claims: Circuit depth reductions reported between factors of 2.5 and 40 relative to standard QAOA and finite-time digitized-adiabatic algorithms (abstract claim).
For a 20-asset portfolio: 7 DCQO steps (twice the depth-per-step of adiabatic steps, effectively reduced to 1 after gate cut-off) matched 80 adiabatic Trotter steps with r(avg) ≈ 0.54 (simulation).
Hardware DCQO (20 qubits on IonQ Aria): r(avg) = 0.40 (unmitigated), r(avg) = 0.50 (with debias error mitigation); simulated value r(avg) ≈ 0.54.

Benchmark over 1000 random Ising instances (10–20 qubits): DCQO (CD-only) shows roughly a 2× improvement in approximation ratio at fixed circuit depth compared to non-CD evolution (reported qualitatively in results).
Hybrid h-DCQO: one variational layer achieved r(avg) ≈ 0.72 on the 20-asset instance; QAOA p=5 achieved r(avg) ≈ 0.73 while QAOA p=1 gave r(avg) ≈ 0.41 (simulation).
Hardware h-DCQO: mitigated r(avg) = 0.58, unmitigated r(avg) = 0.52, simulation r(avg) = 0.73 for the 20-asset instance (reported in Fig. 5(b)).
Gate-angle cutoff threshold of 0.1 was used to omit small rotations; IonQ's minimum resolvable gate angle is noted as 0.00628 (reference).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper demonstrates reductions in circuit depth and improved performance relative to other quantum algorithms (QAOA and digitized-adiabatic protocols) for specific portfolio and Ising instances, and presents experimental results on trapped-ion hardware. However, it does not claim or demonstrate a quantum computational advantage over classical algorithms; claims are about resource compression and improved quantum-algorithmic performance in the NISQ setting rather than superiority to classical methods.
limitations: Reliance on low-depth circuits and current NISQ hardware — circuit depth and coherence time remain limiting factors for larger or deeper implementations (author-stated).
Gap between simulation and hardware results: experimental outcomes required error mitigation to approach simulated performance; mitigation (debias) did not fully close the gap (author-stated).

Hybrid h-DCQO circuits had larger depth than pure DCQO and showed a significant simulation-to-experiment discrepancy, indicating sensitivity to noise and limited current error mitigation (author-stated).
Exact computation of the adiabatic gauge potential is computationally expensive; this work uses a first-order nested-commutator approximation (author-stated).
Selection of Trotter steps and knowledge of where CD terms are most relevant (e.g., near minimum gap) is nontrivial — determining these locations in advance is challenging (author-stated).
Use of a gate-angle cutoff threshold (0.1) to prune small rotations; threshold choice is heuristic and may affect solution quality and gate counts (author-stated).
Hardware-specific transpilation and native-gate mapping (IonQ GPi/GPi2/MS) can influence circuit cost and noise sensitivity; results are tied to the tested trapped-ion device (author-stated).
[inferred] Scalability beyond 20 qubits is untested: empirical results are shown up to 20 qubits, so performance and resource scaling for significantly larger portfolios remain uncertain.
[inferred] The impulse-regime assumption (|λ| << |˙λ| and CD dominance) may not hold universally across problem instances or scheduling choices; applicability across different regimes is limited.
[inferred] Using only first-order CD terms may limit achievable performance for some instances; trade-offs between higher-order CD accuracy and implementation cost are unresolved.
[inferred] Dependence on classical optimizer choices and parameter settings (COBYLA with 200 iterations used) may affect hybrid performance; optimization may get stuck or require more resources.

[inferred] Problem-instance choices and preprocessing: experiments used a specific 20-asset historical dataset and fixed Lagrange multipliers; results may depend on data window, asset selection, and multiplier tuning.
[inferred] The approach was validated primarily on all-to-all Ising instances; behavior on sparse/intermediate-connectivity graphs or other constraint structures is unclear.
[inferred] Shot-limited measurements (5000 shots) and device-imposed limits could restrict statistical confidence and affect mitigation effectiveness.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — DCQO (digitized counterdiabatic optimization) in the impulse regime yields large circuit-depth reductions (reported 2.5–40×) versus digitized-adiabatic evolution and competitive approximation ratios on a 20-asset Markowitz instance.

#idea:hybrid-approach — h-DCQO uses a variational ansatz composed of CD layers with classical optimization (COBYLA) to tune single- and two-body CD parameters, producing improved simulated performance (r(avg) ≈ 0.73 with one layer).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The impulse-regime strategy, gate-angle cutoff, and transpilation to IonQ native gates reduce gate counts and enable execution on a 25-qubit trapped-ion device with debias mitigation (hardware r(avg) reported: DCQO ≈ 0.50, h-DCQO ≈ 0.58).

#limitation:noise — Hardware results are notably worse than simulation (gap between simulated r(avg) and hardware r(avg)), and debias mitigation was required, indicating noise remains a significant limitation for realized performance.
contradictions: The paper claims reduced reliance on classical optimization, yet the hybrid h-DCQO protocol relies on classical optimizers (COBYLA up to 200 iterations) to tune CD parameters; the 'reduced reliance' claim is therefore qualified rather than absolute.

Simulated h-DCQO attains r(avg) ≈ 0.73, but QAOA at p=5 also attains r(avg) ≈ 0.73 in simulation; this parity suggests that the claimed algorithmic advantage over established variational baselines is not uniformly superior across settings.

There is a performance gap between simulation and hardware (e.g., simulated h-DCQO r(avg) ≈ 0.73 vs hardware r(avg) ≈ 0.58), indicating that implementation noise and device realities can undermine the simulated advantages.
